s: You're listening to Short Wave from NPR.
Hey, Short Wavers, Emily Kwong here with producer Hannah Chinn--
，短浪者，艾米丽· 和制片人汉娜·奇恩--
--and a fridge full to the brim of apples that I picked with my family at Rock Hill Orchard in Maryland.
我和我的家人在马里兰州的罗克希尔果园采集的果。
I forgot, Hannah, there's so many varieties out there.
我忘了，汉娜，那里有很多品种。
There's SunCrisp but also Rome and this new apple I hadn't heard of called a Rosalee.
有太阳，还有罗马，还有这个我从未听说过的新果，叫做Rosalee.
I think that's my new favorite.
我认为这是我新最喜欢的。
You know, Emily, what's really cool is that those Rosalee apples that you saw, they're the same Rosalees that I might see apple picking in New York.
你知道，艾米莉，真正的乐趣是，你看到的罗莎莉果是我在纽约看到的罗莎莉。

Yeah, basically, if I buy a Rosalee in a grocery store in New York, and you buy a Rosalee in an orchard in Maryland, our Rosalee apples are going to be genetically the exact same because they're all from the same original plant.
基本上，如果我在纽约的杂货店买Rosalee，你在马里兰的果园买Rosalee，我们的Rosalee 果将是完全相同的基因，因为它们都来自同一个原始植物。
So you're telling me all apples are copies of each other.
所以你告诉我所有的果都是彼此的副本。
Well, in botanist terms, they're propagated.
在植物学上，它们是传播的。
Every leaf has the genetic potential to make a tree.
每个叶子都有基因潜力来制造树。
And she's supervised a lot of propagation in her time because she's the head of the apple breeding program at Cornell AgriTech in Geneva, New York, which is where I met her for this reporting trip.
因为她是日内瓦的康奈尔农业技术学院的果种植项目负责人，纽约，这是我见到她的报道旅行。
So we take a leaf from the tree that we want to propagate-- so in this case, let's say Honeycrisp-- and we put it on a rootstock by matching the bud to the growing material.
因此，我们从树上的叶子中取出我们想要传播的叶子-- 在这种情况下，让我们说蜂蜜 --
And then when that heals in, it's cut off and it makes a new tree.
然后，当它愈合时，它被切断，形成一个新的树。
Oh, this is what people do with houseplant cuttings when they propagate them.
人们在繁殖时会这样做。
They, like, snip off a bit, put it in water.
他们，像，切断一点，把它放在水中。
You're telling me that the new plant is genetically the exact same as the old plant?
你告诉我，新植物的基因与旧植物相同吗？
Yeah, when people do that, they're basically cloning their houseplants.
是的，当人们这样做时，他们基本上是在克隆他们的家园植物。
So when Susan propagates apple trees, she's basically just copy and pasting them.
所以，当苏珊传播果树时，她基本上只是复制和粘贴它们。
And that means all of the apples on that Honeycrisp tree are going to be genetically identical.
这意味着蜂树上的所有的果都将是基因相同的。
So then, if that's the case, Hannah, how do you create a new kind of apple, like that Rosalee apple?
那么，如果是这样，汉娜，你如何创造一种新的果，像那种果？
I know it's a cross between a Honeycrisp and a Fuji, but I gotta admit, I have no idea how that happens.
我知道这是蜜和富士的交叉，但我不得不承认，我不知道这是如何发生的。
And the science of apple breeding is fascinating.
果种植的科学令人惊叹。
Like, Emily, there's 7,500 varieties of apples grown around the world.
I thought I knew a whole bunch of types of apples, but I didn't realize there were thousands.
我以为我知道很多种果，但我没有意识到有数千种。
Most of them, like RubyFrost or SnapDragon, are invented by breeders like Susan.
它们中的大多数，就像RubyFrost或SnapDragon，是由苏珊这样的繁殖者发明的。
She's basically the Willy Wonka of apples.
Wait, I think I've eaten SnapDragons in New York.
And as the Willy Wonka of apples, she's always on the hunt for a better one, because even my favorite apple, Honeycrisp, turns out, it's not perfect.
作为果的威利温卡，她总是在寻找一个更好的，因为即使是我最喜欢的果，事实证明，它不是完美的。
Great name, great marketing, really popular with people.
伟大的名字，伟大的营销，非常受欢迎的人。
But only about 40% of the Honeycrisp makes it from the orchard to the grocery store.
但只有大约40%的蜂蜜从果园到杂货店。

So when breeders are experimenting with apples, oftentimes, they're trying to increase storability or disease resistance, basically to minimize the loss and maximize the benefits of any given apple variety.
所以，当种植者试验果时，他们往往试图提高果的储存能力或抗病性，基本上是为了尽量减少损失和最大限度地提高果品种的好处。
The science of apples, how apples are selected, bred, and grown, and the discoveries that are changing that process.
果的科学，如何选择果，培养，培养，以及改变这一过程的发现。
Plus, how scientists are preserving the apples of the past in hopes they'll lead us to the fruit of the future.
另外，科学家们如何保存过去的果，希望它们能带领我们到未来的果实。
You're listening to Short Wave, the science podcast from NPR.
你正在听"短波"的科学播客。
OK, Hannah, so we're going to talk about apple breeding, how to make new kinds of apples.
哈纳，我们会谈谈果种植，如何制造新的果。
I actually have no idea how this happens-- at all, like zero understanding.
实际上，我不知道这是如何发生的-- 完全，像零理解。
Let's start with, like, the basics, like how apples breed in nature.
让我们从基本上开始，比如果如何在自然中繁殖。
So when an apple tree is still in flower, bees visit, right?
所以当果树还开花时，蜜蜂会来，对吧？
That flower combines its genetic material with the pollen, sheds its petals, and that apple flower becomes an apple, which you can kind of think of like a fertilized ovary.
这朵花将其遗传材料与花粉结合在一起，果花变成了果，像一个受精的卵巢。
Oh, an apple is an ovary?
And then the seed inside that ovary, inside that apple, is totally unique.
卵巢的种子，果的种子，是完全独特的。
Just like you're a genetic combination of your two parents, an apple seed is a genetic combination of its two parents.
就像你是两个父母的遗传组合一样，果种子是两个父母的遗传组合。
And its two parents are like the apple tree and then the pollen from some other tree.
它的父母就像果树，然后是另一棵树的花粉。
But the bees are really busy, right?
但蜜蜂真的很忙，不是吗？
So they bring a lot of different pollen from a lot of different trees.
所以他们从许多不同的树木中带来了很多不同的花粉。
OK, so it's like a Maury Povich episode up in these apples.
好吧，这就像一个毛里·波维奇事件在这些果上。
Maury-- no, it's like the parentage detective of the aughts.
莫里-- 没有，就像是子的亲戚侦探。
Let's talk about apple Willy Wonka land.
让我们谈谈果威利温卡土地。
Susan Brown and her team at Cornell AgriTech are inventing brand-new varieties of apples all themselves.
苏珊·布朗和她在康奈尔农业技术的团队正在发明全新的果品种。
So in order for Susan to create this brand-new apple, this cross between these two different trees, she has to be able to choose the parents.
为了让苏珊创造出这个全新的果，这两个不同的树之间的交叉，她必须能够选择父母。
And that means she has to beat the bees.
这意味着她必须击败蜜蜂。
So, in an orchard, a tree is there, and bees are going to bring pollen.
在果园里，有一棵树，蜜蜂会带来花粉。
But if I take off the petals and the anthers-- that's the part of the flower that attracts the bee--
但如果我取下叶片和，那就是花朵吸引蜜蜂的部分。
You probably know what the petals look like already, but the anthers are the little, almost antenna-looking things in the middle of the flower.
你可能已经知道叶片的样子了，但子是花的中间的小，几乎像天线的东西。
And so that process is called emasculation, which gets a lot of laughs during talks.
这种过程叫做除，在演讲中会得到很多笑容。
So the tree is not, like, appealing to the bee.
所以这棵树对蜜蜂没有吸引力。
So that apple tree is what they call the seed parent.
这棵果树就是他们称之为种子的父母。
And then they pick the other apple they're going to cross it with, which is called the pollen parent.
然后他们选择了他们要交叉的另一个果，叫做花粉母。
So what then do they do?
So a pollen parent, we select the flowers before they open.
我们选择花在它们开放之前。
And we use a screen or a comb, and we comb out the anthers.
我们使用屏幕或，然后我们把子出来。
So they collect pollen in little plastic vials about the size of, like, a film canister.
所以他们把花粉收集到塑料瓶中，像一个电影容器。
苏珊实际上给我看了一些。
It basically looked like maybe a teaspoon, maybe two, of this really, really fine yellow powder.
基本上看起来像一个茶匙，或者两个，这种非常细的黄粉。
And this is enough pollen to pollinate a ton of flowers.
这足够的花粉可以授粉一花。
And then once the flowers are ready, Susan and her team go through all the trees, and-- Emily, get this-- they have to pollinate each individual flower by hand.
然后一旦花朵准备好，苏珊和她的团队穿过所有的树木，他们必须手工授粉每一朵花。
So if we had a flower here, I'd be, like, gently touching the stigma, which is the receptive surface that the pollen grains grow down.
如果我们在这里有一朵花，我会轻轻地触摸污点，这是花粉颗粒生长的接收表面。
So she hand pollinates that stigma in the center of the flower.
因此，她把花的中部的污名手动授粉。
And it's a ton of work.
She brings in her grad students.
They have to pollinate each flower on each tree twice.
他们必须两次对每棵树的每朵花进行授粉。
It all takes place over the span of two weeks, because they have to do it in the span of time where the apples are flowering.
这一切都发生在两个星期的时间内，因为他们必须在果开花的时间内完成。
So they're racing around like bees.
它们就像蜜蜂一样奔跑。
They're impersonating these bees, flying all about, hand pollinating these apple flowers.
他们扮演这些蜜蜂，飞翔，手工授粉这些果花。
The trees bear apple fruit, which have seeds inside.
树上有果果，其中有种子。
And then we collect the seeds.
So right this time of year, we're collecting the fruit.
所以正是这个时候，我们正在收获水果。
And then by hand, we extract the seeds, which are then propagated.
然后用手来，我们将种子提取出来，然后，它们被传播。
Are these the seeds inside the apple fruits?
这些都是果果子里的种子吗？
They have to cut up all the apples and then extract the seeds by hand and then plant them.
他们必须切割所有的果，然后手动提取种子，然后种植它们。
Yeah, so this is also why, on average, it takes maybe 20 years to develop a new apple.
是的，所以这也是为什么，平均来说，开发一个新的果需要20年。
There's a lot of waiting and patience and work involved.
需要很多等待，耐心和工作。
Anyway, Susan will then plant these newfangled seeds in a giant greenhouse.
无论如何，苏珊将把这些新的种子种植在一个巨大的温室里。
OK, and the seeds grow into apple trees.

他们变成了果种子，这些幼儿树，苏珊和她的团队将它们移植到树底，因为它加快了它们的生长过程。

每种种子就像果树枝，生了两棵，三个果，苏珊和她的团队必须尝试。

我创造了数千种混合物，然后，是的，我必须吃它们。
I kind of use the human example that, as a breeder, I get to do thousands because I want that one really bright child, the shining star of apples.
我用人类的例子来说明，作为种植者，我可以做成千上万，因为我想要一个非常明亮的孩子，
I-- you know, I have two wonderful children.
我--你知道的，我有两个很棒的孩子。
My apples I don't have to keep.

她把真正的坏果扔出去。

我可以问-- 你说你必须吃所有这些数千...
I'm sure that there are some that are not good.

这就像美国偶像，但是果品味。

但整个过程--手工授粉，种子提取，种子生长，品味测试--
So Susan is researching a different way to do it through apple DNA testing.
苏珊正在通过果DNA测试来研究一种不同的方法。
The idea behind this research is that you could look at each apple tree and read its gene markers like a book.
这项研究背后的想法是，你可以看看每棵果树，和阅读它的基因标记像一本书。
That way, before you even have to taste each apple, you know what it'd be like, and you could potentially select for specific markers, like whether an apple is red or yellow.
这样，在你甚至不得不品尝每个果之前，你知道这会是什么样子，你可能会选择特定的标记，比如果是红色还是黄色。
Let's see, on the genetic level, whether we can find a strand of DNA that matches whether it's red or yellow.
让我们看，在遗传层面上，如果我们能找到一个与红色或黄色相匹配的DNA。
And it's like marking a deck of cards.
You can use that marker to select at the seedling stage-- so before they even fruit.
你可以使用这个标记在种植阶段进行选择。

我认为这节省了很多时间和不好的果品味。

所以这个过程已经实施了吗？

比如，为什么她现在不做这件事？

这就是我在这个节目中学到的。

54,000 genes, that is a lot to map.

但也意味着科学家们还有太多的可能性去探索。

果的惊人之处是它的广泛的遗传多样性。

他是一位植物遗传学家，也是苏珊的前学生。

它就像一个巨大的档案库，像诺亚的果箱。
